Wisconsin property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Board of review meets annually during the 45-day period beginning on the 4th Monday of April, no sooner than 7 days after the assessment roll's last open-for-examination day. (Wis. Stat. 70.47(1); source)
  • Notice of intent to object must be given to the board clerk (written or oral) at least 48 hours before the board's first scheduled meeting, subject to good-cause waiver during the first 2 hours. (Wis. Stat. 70.47(7)(a); source)
  • A written objection must be filed with the board clerk within the first 2 hours of the board's first scheduled meeting (waivable only for extraordinary circumstances). (Wis. Stat. 70.47(7)(a); source)
  • DOR must receive a written complaint within 20 days after delivery of the board of review determination, or within 30 days after the mailing date on the clerk's affidavit. (2026 Guide for Property Owners (WI DOR), sec. X.E.2 (sec. 70.47(12)); source)
  • A board of review determination may be appealed by certiorari to circuit court within 90 days after receiving notice from the board. (2026 Guide for Property Owners (WI DOR), sec. X.E.1 (sec. 70.47(13)); source)
  • A claim for excessive assessment must be served on the municipal clerk (or county clerk in a county assessor system) by January 31 of the year the tax is payable. (Wis. Stat. 74.37(2)(b)5.; source)
  • The municipality must allow or disallow an excessive assessment claim within 90 days; if disallowed, the claimant has 90 days after receiving notice to sue in circuit court. (Wis. Stat. 74.37(3)(b),(d); source)
  • Assessment ratio is the relationship between a parcel's assessed value and its fair market value (e.g., $140,000 assessed on a $150,000 sale is 93%); assessment level is the district-wide assessed-to-equalized-value relationship. (2026 Guide for Property Owners (WI DOR), Glossary; source)
  • A county treasurer may file a list of tax-certificate parcels for in rem foreclosure after 2 years from the tax certificate date (1 year in specified cases, including certain cities and counties of 750,000+). (Wis. Stat. 75.521(3)(a); source)
  • Petition and parcel list must be mailed by registered or certified mail to each owner and mortgagee of record. (Wis. Stat. 75.521(3)(c); source)

Wisconsin Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Wisconsin Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Wisconsin Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • An exempt homestead of a resident owner who occupies it is exempt from execution, judgment liens and creditor debts up to $75,000, except mortgages, mechanics' and purchase money liens and taxes. (Wis. Stat. 815.20(1); source)
  • The exemption extends to sale proceeds up to $75,000 while held with intent to procure another homestead, for 2 years. (Wis. Stat. 815.20(1); source)
  • Each spouse may claim up to $75,000 on land owned jointly or as marital property. (Wis. Stat. 815.20(1); source)
  • A conveyance that alienates a married person's interest in a homestead must be signed (or joined in) by each spouse, except conveyances between spouses. (Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(f); source)

What is the Wisconsin homestead exemption?

The Wisconsin homestead exemption is a creditor shield, and it protects up to $75,000 of a homeowner's interest in the home they live in. It sits in Wis. Stat. 815.20, which says an exempt homestead chosen and occupied by a resident owner is exempt from execution, from the lien of every judgment, and from liability for the owner's debts up to that amount.

The shield has limits. Mortgages, laborers' liens, mechanics' liens, purchase money liens and taxes still attach to the property. A judgment creditor who holds none of those cannot force a sale of equity inside the $75,000 line.

Many Wisconsin owners search for "homestead exemption" expecting a property tax break. That relief exists under a different name, covered further down. This page keeps the two apart so you know which one applies to your sale.

How much of a Wisconsin home does the exemption protect?

Each owner is protected up to $75,000, and a married couple can double that on jointly owned or marital property land. The table below pulls the main numbers from the statutes and from the Department of Revenue.

ItemRuleSource
Exempt amountUp to $75,000 against execution, judgment liens and debtsWis. Stat. 815.20(1)
SpousesEach spouse may claim up to $75,000 on land owned jointly or as marital propertyWis. Stat. 815.20(1)
Liens that still attachMortgages, laborers', mechanics' and purchase money liens, and taxesWis. Stat. 815.20(1)
Land coveredAt least 0.25 acre if available, no more than 40 acresWis. Stat. 990.01(14)
Sale proceedsProtected up to $75,000 for 2 years while held to buy another homesteadWis. Stat. 815.20(1)
Homestead credit, tax year 2025Household income under $24,680, maximum credit $1,168DOR Fact Sheet 1116

The 0.25 acre and 40 acre figures come from Wis. Stat. 990.01(14), which defines an exempt homestead as the dwelling plus the land reasonably needed to use it as a home.

What kinds of homes and owners qualify in Wisconsin?

The dwelling can be a house, condominium, mobile home, manufactured home, house trailer or cooperative unit. The definition in s. 990.01(14) lists each of those forms.

  • Tenants in common qualify when they live on the land with the consent of their co-owners, and so does any estate less than a fee.
  • Court annotations to the statute say a land contract buyer holds an interest large enough to support the exemption.
  • The annotations also say rent from a rented part of the homestead stays exempt.
  • Occupancy matters. A court of appeals decision recorded under the statute says an owner who leaves with no plan to return and no plan to sell and buy a new home loses the protection.

A temporary move does not break the exemption when the owner intends to return. The statute says a temporary removal with the intention to reoccupy does not impair the exemption, and a court of appeals decision in the annotations says the exemption is read broadly to protect the homeowner.

What happens to the exemption when I sell my Wisconsin home?

The exemption follows the money. The statute extends it to sale proceeds up to $75,000 for 2 years, as long as you hold the money with the intention of buying another homestead.

That two-year window is useful for an owner who is behind on debts and wants to sell quickly. A decision cited in the annotations holds that owners who permanently leave a home that is for sale, planning to put the proceeds toward a new home, keep the exemption in those proceeds. Keep the sale money in an account that is easy to trace, and speak with a Wisconsin attorney before you move it.

Equity also affects how clean the title is. The annotations report a Wisconsin Supreme Court holding that when a debtor's equity is under the exempt amount, the home is fully exempt and a docketed judgment has nothing to attach to, so the seller can deliver clear title. When equity is higher, a judgment lien can reach the part above the line. If a creditor will not release a lien on a home worth less than $75,000, s. 815.20(2) lets the owner ask a court for declaratory relief after the creditor ignores a demand for a recordable release for 10 days.

Does a spouse have to sign the deed?

Yes, in most cases. Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(f) requires a conveyance of a married person's interest in a homestead to be signed, or joined in by a separate conveyance, by each spouse. Conveyances between spouses are the exception.

A purchase money mortgage on that property needs only the purchaser's signature. The rule applies even when only one spouse appears on the title. If a spouse is separated or hard to reach, sort that out before the closing date.

Is the homestead exemption the same as Wisconsin property tax relief?

No. The exemption protects equity from creditors. Property tax relief comes through credits, and the two main ones are the homestead credit and the lottery and gaming credit.

The Department of Revenue describes the homestead credit as relief for people with lower incomes who own or rent a home that pays Wisconsin property tax. For tax year 2025 the main requirements are:

  • You occupied and owned or rented a dwelling subject to Wisconsin property taxes during 2025.
  • You were a Wisconsin resident for all of 2025 and 18 or older on December 31, 2025.
  • Household income was under $24,680, after a $500 deduction for each qualifying dependent.
  • You, or your spouse, had earned income, was disabled, or was 62 or older at the end of 2025.
  • You will not claim the farmland preservation credit or the veterans and surviving spouses property tax credit for the same year.

The maximum credit is $1,168. Property taxes count when levied for 2025, no matter when you pay them. Schedule H-EZ is open only to people who did not sell their home during 2025, so a seller will usually file the longer Schedule H. The Department lists a phone line at (608) 266-2486 for questions.

How does the lottery and gaming credit work if I sell?

The lottery and gaming credit goes with the property, and it belongs on your list when you prorate taxes at closing. The Department of Revenue page says the credit remains with a qualifying property after a sale and comes off the net tax payable on the next bill.

  • To qualify, you must be a Wisconsin resident who owns the dwelling and uses it as a primary residence on the January 1 certification date.
  • A person can claim only one primary residence. Rental units, vacant land and garages do not qualify.
  • A buyer who is not living there as a primary residence files Form LC-400 with the county treasurer to remove the credit.
  • A buyer who purchased after January 1 can apply if the prior owner used the home as a primary residence on January 1.

If your bill is missing the credit, you can apply to the municipal treasurer by January 31 after you receive the bill. A late claim goes to the Department of Revenue by October 1.

What should I check before accepting a cash offer?

Check three things before you sign: who holds liens, whether every spouse will sign, and where the proceeds will go. Each connects to the exemption.

  • Ask the register of deeds in your county for a copy of any recorded judgment, mortgage or lien against the property.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the current tax bill so the credit and proration are accurate.
  • Make sure the contract and deed carry the signature of each spouse where s. 706.02(1)(f) requires it.
  • Plan where the sale money will sit for the 2-year proceeds window.

A Wisconsin owner who sells as-is still has to deliver a condition report on one-to-four unit property within 10 days after the contract is accepted, unless an exemption applies. Raise that early so there is no surprise at closing.

More questions about Wisconsin Homestead Exemption

How much is the Wisconsin homestead exemption?

It is $75,000 per owner. A married couple can each claim up to $75,000 on land they own jointly or as marital property, under Wis. Stat. 815.20(1). Mortgages, mechanics' liens, purchase money liens and taxes sit outside the shield.

Does the exemption protect me if I sell the house?

Yes, for a limited time. Sale proceeds stay exempt up to $75,000 for 2 years while you hold them to buy another homestead. If you spend the money on something else, that protection can be lost.

Is the homestead credit the same as the exemption?

No. The homestead credit is a Department of Revenue credit for lower-income households. For tax year 2025, household income must be under $24,680 and the maximum credit is $1,168. The exemption is a creditor protection with no income test.

Does my spouse need to sign if only my name is on the deed?

In most cases yes. Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(f) requires each spouse to sign or join in a conveyance of a married person's interest in a homestead, except for conveyances between spouses. Ask the title company to review the deed before closing.

What if a creditor has a judgment against me?

The judgment lien cannot attach to equity inside the $75,000 exemption. If your home is worth less than that and the creditor will not release the lien within 10 days after a demand, s. 815.20(2) lets you ask the court for declaratory relief. Confirm the details with a Wisconsin attorney.

title: Wisconsin Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Wisconsin Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Wisconsin
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Wisconsin Estate and Inheritance Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Wisconsin Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Wisconsin Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Wisconsin House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • There is no Wisconsin inheritance tax for decedents dying on or after January 1, 1992. (DOR Estates, Trusts, and Fiduciaries; source)
Selling in Wisconsin?
We buy Wisconsin houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Wisconsin have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

No. The Wisconsin Department of Revenue states that there is no Wisconsin estate tax for deaths occurring on or after January 1, 2008, and its tax bulletin lists an inheritance tax return only for deaths before January 1, 1992. A family that inherits a Wisconsin house from a recent death pays neither state tax just because the deed changes hands.

Three other costs can still reach an heir who wants to sell: the federal estate tax on very large estates, income tax on any gain from the sale, and the county transfer fee collected when a deed is recorded. Each one follows its own rules, and the sections below take them in turn. If the death happened before the cutoff years above, ask the Department of Revenue which return applied to that estate.

Does the federal estate tax apply to a Wisconsin house?

Only when the whole estate is very large. The IRS says a return is required when the gross estate, plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, is worth more than the filing threshold for the year of death. That threshold is $15,000,000 for 2026, $13,990,000 for 2025 and $13,610,000 for 2024.

The gross estate counts everything the person owned or had certain interests in, valued at fair market value on the date of death. Deductions then come off for mortgages and other debts, administration expenses, and property that passes to a surviving spouse or a qualified charity. The IRS adds that most relatively simple estates do not need to file. For scale, the Census Bureau puts the median value of an owner-occupied home in Wisconsin at $266,500 for 2020 to 2024, so one house sits far below the 2026 threshold.

A surviving spouse may elect to carry over the decedent's unused exemption, and that election is made on a timely filed estate tax return. If the Wisconsin estate you are settling is anywhere near the threshold, a federal return is a job for an estate attorney or tax preparer, not a title company.

What income tax do heirs owe when they sell an inherited Wisconsin house?

They owe income tax on any gain, and the Wisconsin return gives a partial break. Department of Revenue Publication 103 says gains and losses from selling capital assets are reportable for both Wisconsin and federal income tax, and that Wisconsin generally allows a deduction for 30% of the net capital gain from assets held more than one year. The publication is written for 2025 returns.

The gain is the sale price less basis. IRS Topic 703 explains that basis is usually what you paid, and that property received by inheritance follows the separate rules in IRS Publication 551. Get the basis figure from the estate's tax preparer before you compare offers on the house, because it drives the tax result.

  • Individual heirs report the sale on Wisconsin Schedule WD. Estates and trusts use Schedule 2WD with Form 2, Wisconsin Fiduciary Income Tax for Estates and Trusts.
  • A net capital loss can offset up to $3,000 of other income ($1,500 if married filing separately) on a Wisconsin return, beginning with tax year 2023. Larger losses carry forward.
  • Wisconsin and federal basis can differ for certain assets, so ask the preparer whether the Wisconsin figure needs an adjustment.

How much is the Wisconsin transfer fee when an inherited house sells?

The fee is 30 cents for each $100 of value, and the seller pays it. Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) places the fee on the grantor, has the register of deeds collect it when the deed is submitted for recording, and requires a transfer return signed by grantor and grantee. On a $250,000 sale the fee is $750.

Passing the house to heirs is a different event from selling it. A conveyance by will, descent or survivorship is exempt under Wis. Stat. 77.25(11). The Department of Revenue's transfer return FAQ is plain that a sale under a will is not exempt, and the sale price is the value that carries the fee.

TransferFee treatmentRule
Estate or heirs sell to a buyerFee on the sale priceWis. Stat. 77.22(1); DOR FAQ
House passes to heirs by will, descent or survivorshipExemptWis. Stat. 77.25(11)
Heir pays siblings or the estate to take the houseFee on the amount paid, exemption for the restDOR FAQ
Trustee deeds to a beneficiary for no paymentExemptWis. Stat. 77.25(9)
Gift between parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, for nominal or no considerationExemptWis. Stat. 77.25(8)

Transfer returns are filed electronically unless the Department of Revenue grants a hardship waiver. When a deed claims an exemption, the reason is stated on the face of the deed by reference to the subsection of 77.25.

Can a small Wisconsin estate skip probate before the house is sold?

Only if the estate is small. Wis. Stat. 867.03 lets an heir, the trustee of a revocable trust, a person named in the will as personal representative, or the decedent's guardian collect property by affidavit when the decedent's property subject to administration in Wisconsin does not exceed $50,000 in gross value. A house worth more than that by itself puts the estate outside the affidavit route.

The statute also blocks a person named as personal representative from receiving real property by affidavit, unless that person is also an heir, a trustee of a revocable trust created by the decedent, or the decedent's guardian. Transfers to a named personal representative who is not one of those people wait 30 days after the affidavit is received. Larger estates need a probate case. Ask the probate office of the circuit court in the county where the decedent lived what the court needs before a buyer can close.

What should Wisconsin heirs check before accepting a cash offer on an inherited house?

A cash purchase is still a sale, so the same fee and gain rules apply. Work through this short list before you sign:

  • Ask the estate's tax preparer for the basis in the house and an estimate of the gain, and which schedule reports it.
  • Ask the county register of deeds how the transfer return and exemption number should read on any deed that moves title to heirs without payment.
  • Confirm in writing who has authority to sign for the estate, and ask the circuit court's probate office what proof of that authority a buyer will need.
  • Ask the buyer to show the transfer fee on the closing statement, since the fee is imposed on the seller.
  • If any heir is buying out the others, tell the preparer, because the payment is subject to the transfer fee.

More questions about Wisconsin Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Wisconsin have an inheritance tax?

No. The Department of Revenue lists an inheritance tax return only for deaths before January 1, 1992, and says there is no Wisconsin estate tax for deaths on or after January 1, 2008. Heirs who inherit a Wisconsin house from a recent death owe neither tax on the transfer.

How large must an estate be before a federal estate tax return is required?

For a 2026 death, the filing threshold is $15,000,000. The IRS counts the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption against that figure. Most relatively simple estates do not need to file.

Do heirs pay tax when they sell an inherited house in Wisconsin?

They can owe income tax on the gain, which is the sale price less basis. Wisconsin generally allows a deduction for 30% of net capital gain from assets held more than one year. Ask the estate's tax preparer for the basis and the likely result.

Is the Wisconsin transfer fee due when a house passes under a will?

No. A conveyance by will, descent or survivorship is exempt under Wis. Stat. 77.25(11). The fee of 30 cents per $100 applies when the house is sold, and the sale price is the value that carries it.

Can a Wisconsin estate use an affidavit instead of probate for a house?

Only when the decedent's property subject to administration in Wisconsin does not exceed $50,000 in gross value. A person named in the will as personal representative cannot receive real property by affidavit unless that person is also an heir, a trustee of the decedent's revocable trust, or the decedent's guardian.

title: Wisconsin Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House
content:
Wisconsin Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in Wisconsin
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Wisconsin Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House sale
  • Turn the Wisconsin Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Wisconsin House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • A civil eviction action may be commenced by the person entitled to possession or the written agent. (Wis. Stat. 799.40(1); source)
  • Appeal of an eviction judgment must be initiated within 15 days. (Wis. Stat. 799.445; source)
  • The sheriff must execute a writ of restitution within 10 days of receipt. (Wis. Stat. 799.45(5)(a); source)
Selling in Wisconsin?
We buy Wisconsin houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does an eviction case move through Wisconsin courts?

It runs as a small claims case in the county circuit court. The Wisconsin court system's small claims self-help page says eviction actions are heard in small claims regardless of the rent claimed, and it links an eviction guide and a forms assistant. Chapter 799 of the Wisconsin Statutes governs the procedure.

Under Wis. Stat. 799.40, the person entitled to possession, or an agent authorized in writing, starts the case. The landlord can add a claim for money tied to the tenant's occupancy, such as unpaid rent, and the complaint must state that claim separately. The complaint under 799.41 must be in writing, name the parties, identify the property (a street name and number is enough), and state the facts that justify removal.

A party may appear alone or through an attorney. Under 799.06(2), an agent or authorized employee of a company counts as the company appearing in its own person.

What are the Wisconsin eviction deadlines after a case is filed?

The statutes set several short clocks, summarized below. Dates run from the court's own paperwork, so read the summons and any order for the exact days in your county.

StepRuleStatute
Summons return dateSet 5 to 25 days after the summons issues; tenant served at least 5 days before the return date799.05(3)(b)
Judgment and writIf the landlord is entitled to possession, the court enters judgment for restitution and orders a writ issued at once799.44(1), (2)
Hardship stayCourt may stay the writ up to 30 days, on condition that rent and occupancy charges are paid799.44(3)
Emergency assistance stayCourt stays the case while the tenant applies, for no more than 10 working days, and not after a writ issues799.40(4)(a)
Sheriff actsExecutes the writ within 10 days of receiving it; a writ received more than 30 days after issuance is not executed799.45(5)(a); 799.44(2)
AppealMust be started within 15 days of the judgment or order799.445

Can a Wisconsin tenant delay or stop an eviction?

In limited ways. The court can grant a hardship stay of up to 30 days from the order for judgment, but the stay depends on the tenant paying all rent and charges due at judgment and the reasonable value of occupancy during the stay. The judge may also require a bond. If the tenant misses a condition, the landlord files an affidavit and the writ can issue right away.

An appeal does not freeze the case by itself. Under Wis. Stat. 799.445, a tenant's appeal stays enforcement only if the tenant files an undertaking with surety approved by the judge. The undertaking covers appeal costs, rent and damages that accrue during the appeal. If the tenant then misses rent, the guaranteed payment goes straight to the landlord and the stay ends so the sheriff can execute the writ.

  • A landlord who accepts past due rent after serving notice or after filing cannot be forced into dismissal on that ground (799.40(1m)).
  • An earlier waiver of a lease breach is not a defense to eviction or to a damages claim (799.40(1s)).
  • If the case is an eviction of a tenant after a foreclosure sale, the complaint must say so (799.41(2)), and the court stays the case against a foreclosed homeowner as provided in Wis. Stat. 846.40(9) (799.40(4)(b)).

What happens to belongings when the Wisconsin sheriff executes a writ?

The sheriff removes the tenant and anyone claiming under the tenant, using reasonable force when needed, and then handles the property under Wis. Stat. 799.45. The landlord has two choices on belongings. By default, the sheriff moves the property to a place of safekeeping in the county and mails the tenant a written notice of its location within 3 days. The sheriff may ask the landlord for a deposit toward moving costs first.

The alternative is for the landlord to tell the sheriff, when delivering the writ, that the landlord will remove and store or dispose of the property under Wis. Stat. 704.05(5). In that case the sheriff supervises if asked.

  • Property the sheriff judges to have no monetary value can be taken to a refuse site, with notice to the tenant within 3 days.
  • Prescription medication and prescription medical equipment must be held for 7 days after the landlord discovers it, and returned promptly if the tenant asks before disposal.
  • Before disposing of a manufactured home, mobile home or titled vehicle, the landlord must notify the tenant and any secured party the landlord knows about.
  • A landlord that will not store belongings must tell the tenant in writing when the lease is signed or renewed.

What should a Wisconsin owner gather before filing an eviction?

The court will want proof that the notice was proper and delivered by a listed method, so keep the paper trail together. The checklist below follows the statutes rather than any local form.

  • The signed lease or rental terms, including any signed term on showing the premises or storing belongings.
  • A rent ledger that separates rent from late fees, since the notice statute defines rent to include late fees on past due rent.
  • A copy of the notice and proof of how it was delivered. For certified mail, the post office's proof of mailing is enough under 799.40(1g).
  • The street address of the rental, which is enough to identify the property in the complaint.
  • A plan for the tenant's belongings: sheriff storage, or the owner's own removal and storage under 704.05(5).

Your county circuit court clerk can say which forms and fees apply locally. Ask the clerk before filing.

Can an owner sell a Wisconsin house that has a tenant or an eviction pending?

A sale does not erase the tenancy. Wis. Stat. 704.05(2) gives a tenant who is not in default exclusive possession until the lease expires or a periodic tenancy is terminated, and lets the landlord show the premises to purchasers on advance notice at reasonable times. The statute applies unless a signed lease provision says otherwise.

An owner weighing a sale should compare two paths. One is to finish the notice and court steps above and hand over an empty house. The other is to sell with the tenant in place, which skips the court steps. The timeline for the first path depends on the return date the court sets and, after judgment, the sheriff's 10-day window, and those dates are set case by case.

More questions about Wisconsin Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does an eviction take in Wisconsin?

The statutes set pieces of the timeline, not one total. The summons return date falls 5 to 25 days after issue, and after judgment the sheriff has 10 days from receiving the writ to execute it. A hardship stay of up to 30 days or an appeal can add time.

Can a Wisconsin tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent?

Paying late rent after notice does not by itself end the case, because a landlord who accepts past due rent after notice or filing cannot be forced to dismiss. A hardship stay of up to 30 days is possible at judgment, and it depends on paying rent and occupancy charges.

How long does a tenant have to appeal a Wisconsin eviction judgment?

Fifteen days from the judgment or order. An appeal pauses enforcement only if the tenant files an undertaking with approved surety covering costs, rent and damages during the appeal.

Who removes a tenant after the court rules for the landlord?

The sheriff. The court orders a writ of restitution, the writ goes to the sheriff, and the sheriff removes the tenant and anyone claiming under the tenant. The sheriff must execute the writ within 10 days of receiving it.

Can a Wisconsin landlord ask for back rent in the eviction case?

Yes. Wis. Stat. 799.40(2) allows the landlord to join a claim arising from the tenant's possession or occupancy, such as rent owed, and the complaint states that claim separately from the request for possession.

  • The designation is not effective unless recorded with the register of deeds (with fees) before the death of the sole or last owner. (Wis. Stat. 705.15(2)(c); source)
  • The designation does not affect ownership until death and can be revoked by a compliant recorded instrument acknowledged after the original and recorded before death. (Wis. Stat. 705.15(3)(a); source)
  • On death, the property passes subject to liens to surviving beneficiaries (and issue of a predeceased one), otherwise to the owner's estate. (Wis. Stat. 705.15(4); source)
  • A TOD beneficiary's interest may be confirmed under s. 863.27, 865.201 or 867.046. (Wis. Stat. 705.15(5); source)
  • Conveyances solely designating a TOD beneficiary, and TOD transfers at death, are exempt from the transfer fee. (Wis. Stat. 77.25(10m),(11m); source)

Wisconsin Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Wisconsin rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Wisconsin?

It is a recorded document that names who receives a piece of Wisconsin real estate when the owner dies, with no probate case needed for that property. The law behind it is Wis. Stat. 705.15, which describes a "TOD beneficiary designation" made on a recorded document. People call that document a transfer on death deed, and the register of deeds treats it as one.

The statute covers five kinds of ownership. An owner can use it for any of these:

  • An interest held by one individual and by no one else
  • A fractional interest held as a tenant in common
  • An interest held by a spouse as marital property
  • An interest held by spouses as survivorship marital property
  • An interest held by two or more people as joint tenants

Transfer happens on the death of the sole owner, or on the death of the last of several owners to die. Until then the beneficiary has no ownership.

What must a Wisconsin TOD designation say?

The document has to name the owner or owners, name the beneficiary, and state that the transfer takes effect only on the owner's death. When the property is marital property held by a spouse, both spouses with an interest must sign. These requirements come from section 705.15(2)(a).

The wording is flexible. An owner can use the words "transfer on death" or "pay on death," or the letters TOD or POD, placed after the owner's name and ahead of the beneficiary's name. An owner may list primary beneficiaries and also contingent ones who take if a primary beneficiary does not survive. The designation can sit on the original deed that gave the owner title, or on a later document signed and recorded by the sole owner or by all surviving owners.

Capacity matters too. The mental capacity needed to sign or cancel a designation is the same as the capacity needed to make or revoke a will under s. 853.01.

Recording is what makes the document work. A designation is ineffective unless the document, and the recording fees, are submitted to the register of deeds in the county where the land sits before the sole or last owner dies. A signed paper in a drawer does nothing.

Can the owner still sell or change the plan after signing?

Yes. Under section 705.15(3)(a), a designation does not affect ownership until the sole or last owner dies, even if the document says something different. The owner keeps full control, and subsection (3)(c) adds that the rule does not limit a transfer made during the owner's life. A sale, a gift or a mortgage during life is still possible.

To cancel or change a designation, the owner records a new instrument. It must meet every one of these tests:

  • It is a new designation document, an instrument of revocation, or a lifetime deed that expressly revokes the earlier recorded document, in whole or in part
  • The owner acknowledged it after acknowledging the earlier document
  • It reaches the register of deeds in the property's county before the sole or last owner dies

When several owners signed one designation, an owner's revocation does not undo the designation as to another owner's interest. For joint tenants or spouses with survivorship marital property, the designation is revoked only if all living joint tenants or spouses revoke it.

What happens to the house when the owner dies?

Ownership passes to the surviving beneficiaries, subject to any lien or encumbrance on the property. If a named beneficiary died first, that beneficiary's issue who would take under s. 854.06(3) step in. If nobody qualifies, the interest goes to the deceased owner's estate. Chapter 854 applies to these transfers.

The beneficiary then needs paper proof of title. Section 705.15(5) points to three routes: s. 863.27, s. 865.201 or s. 867.046. The last one is handled at the register of deeds. The beneficiary gives the register an application with the decedent's name, residence and address, the applicant's details and the date of death, signed and sworn. For real estate the applicant adds the most recent property tax bill, a legal description and a copy of the deed that created the TOD interest. Once recorded, the application ends the decedent's interest with the same force as a court order from the probate court of the decedent's home county.

Timing rules to know:

  • If the beneficiary or personal representative has not started a confirmation within 90 days of death, any interested person may apply under s. 867.046(2m)
  • A claim to recover real property that went to a TOD beneficiary is barred unless a complaint and a lis pendens are filed within 120 days after the death (s. 705.15(8))
  • A good-faith buyer or lender who deals with the petitioner takes title free of claims by the decedent's estate (s. 867.046(6))

What fees and transfer taxes apply to a Wisconsin TOD?

Recording costs $30 per document under s. 59.43(2)(ag), and the register may refuse a document that does not meet its format rules. Those rules include a blank 3-inch by 3-inch space in the upper right corner of page one, the drafter's name, a legal description, no Social Security number, and a parcel identification number in counties that require one.

The state real estate transfer fee does not apply here. Under s. 77.25(10m), a conveyance made solely to designate a TOD beneficiary is exempt, and under s. 77.25(11m) so is the nonprobate transfer at death. The Department of Revenue tells filers to file a Real Estate Transfer Return in My Tax Account when removing a decedent's interest, pick "Termination of Decedent's Interest," and claim exemption 11m if a TOD document was recorded before death. The filer enters the recorded document number and an estimated value taken from the most recent tax bill. Questions go to RETR@wisconsin.gov or (608) 264-6885.

StepWho or whereAuthority
Sign and record the designation while aliveRegister of deeds, property's countyWis. Stat. 705.15(2)(c)
Pay the recording fee of $30 per documentRegister of deedsWis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag)
Claim the transfer fee exemptionDocument and transfer returnWis. Stat. 77.25(10m), (11m)
Confirm the beneficiary's interest after deathRegister of deeds applicationWis. Stat. 867.046(2)
Bring any competing claimCourt complaint and lis pendens within 120 daysWis. Stat. 705.15(8)

What if the beneficiary wants to sell the Wisconsin house?

The beneficiary can sell once the interest is confirmed and any liens are dealt with. Because the property passes subject to liens, a mortgage or tax debt does not vanish at death. It stays on the title until paid, so a payoff figure belongs in the first conversation with a title company.

A beneficiary who lives far away or inherits a house that needs repairs may want to sell quickly. Line up the confirmation paperwork first: the register of deeds application, the recent tax bill and the recorded designation.

When the estate has an open informal administration, the Wisconsin court system offers form PR-1827, a statement of termination or confirmation of interests in property tied to ss. 705.15, 865.20 and 865.201. An attorney or personal representative completes it, and a certified copy or duplicate original may be recorded with the register of deeds. An attorney can say which path suits a particular family.

More questions about Wisconsin Transfer on Death Deed

Does a Wisconsin transfer on death deed avoid probate?

Yes, for the property named in it. Section 705.15 lets the property pass to the designated beneficiary without probate, but only if the designation was recorded with the register of deeds before the last owner died. Other assets without a beneficiary can still need a probate case.

Does the beneficiary have to consent to the designation?

No. The statute requires the owner's signature, plus both spouses' signatures for marital property, and says nothing about a beneficiary signing. The designation can be revoked by a recorded instrument without the beneficiary's involvement.

How much does it cost to record a TOD designation in Wisconsin?

The register of deeds charges $30 per recorded document under s. 59.43(2)(ag). The state transfer fee does not apply because s. 77.25(10m) exempts a conveyance made solely to designate a TOD beneficiary. Ask the register of deeds in the property's county about any local recording requirements.

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

The property goes to the predeceased beneficiary's issue who would take under s. 854.06(3). If no beneficiary or qualifying issue survives all owners, it passes to the estate of the sole or last owner. A contingent beneficiary named in the document takes before that point.

Can the owner still sell the house after naming a beneficiary?

Yes. The designation does not change ownership until death, and s. 705.15(3)(c) leaves lifetime transfers untouched. A sale during life ends the owner's interest, so nothing is left for the designation to pass at death. Ask an attorney before signing a deed.

How does probate work in Wisconsin?

Probate in Wisconsin is a court-supervised process that moves a dead person's assets to the people entitled to them. The Wisconsin court system self-help page says Wisconsin Statutes chapters 851 through 882 govern probate actions.

The Wisconsin Register in Probate Association explains the process in its Guide to Informal Estate Administration, revised November 2025 and posted by the courts. Administration gives notice to creditors and interested persons, identifies heirs and beneficiaries, collects and inventories assets, pays taxes and claims, and transfers what remains.

The case is filed in the county where the decedent lived. If the person was not a Wisconsin resident, the application can go to any Wisconsin county where the person owned property.

Which type of Wisconsin probate fits an estate with a house?

That depends on the size of the estate, whether there is a will, and whether the heirs agree. The table compares the main paths described in the court guide and the statutes.

PathWhen it appliesSource
Transfer by affidavitProperty subject to administration of $50,000 or less in gross valueWis. Stat. 867.03(1g)
Summary settlement$50,000 or less with a surviving spouse, domestic partner or minor childrenCourt guide
Summary assignment$50,000 or less, for estates that cannot use summary settlementCourt guide
Informal administrationSupervised by the Probate Registrar, no continuous court supervisionCourt guide
Formal administrationContinuous court supervision, and an attorney is neededCourt guide
Register of deeds confirmationSpouse or beneficiary of a marital property agreement or TOD interestWis. Stat. 867.046(2)

Court staff cannot tell you which path to pick. The guide says that choice is a legal decision and suggests talking to an attorney, especially when heirs disagree, claims are disputed or taxes are an issue.

What if the owner died without a will in Wisconsin?

The estate still goes through administration, and the heirs are set by statute. The court guide points to Wis. Stat. 852.01 for who counts as an heir when there is no will, and its chart treats a surviving domestic partner the same as a surviving spouse.

The guide also explains how shares split. Under the per stirpes rule, property divides at each generation, with one share for each surviving person and one for each deceased person, and a deceased person's share passes to that person's issue. With three children, the children's portion divides into thirds, and if one child has died leaving two children, that third splits between the two grandchildren.

Informal administration of an intestate estate can be denied when the heirs do not all consent in writing, or when an interested person demands formal proceedings. Any heir can demand formal proceedings, which moves the case in front of a judge.

Can a personal representative sell an inherited Wisconsin house?

Yes, once the court has appointed the personal representative and issued letters. Being named in a will is only a nomination. The guide says the Probate Registrar or a judge must appoint you, and the proof of that appointment is a document called Domiciliary Letters.

  • Sign the deed with the legal description of the land, not the street address. The guide warns that a mistake in the legal description can affect ownership.
  • Take the original will and any codicils to the court. The guide says they must be delivered.
  • Plan to inventory the home at its fair market value on the date of death.

A named personal representative also cannot use the small estate affidavit to take real estate. Wis. Stat. 867.03(1h) bars that unless the person is also an heir, a trustee of the decedent's revocable trust, or the decedent's guardian.

What does the Wisconsin small estate affidavit allow?

It lets certain people collect money and property of the decedent without opening a court case, if the estate is $50,000 or less in gross value. Under Wis. Stat. 867.03(1g), an heir, the trustee of a revocable trust, a person named in the will as personal representative, or the decedent's guardian may use it.

  • The affidavit must describe the property and give its value, and it must state the total value of the estate.
  • A person named in the will who is not also an heir must wait 30 days before the holder of property transfers it under the affidavit.
  • If the decedent or the decedent's spouse ever received long-term care program services or medical assistance benefits, the affiant must first give notice to the Department of Health Services and attach proof of mail delivery.

The court guide notes that the State Bar of Wisconsin maintains the affidavit form and that the person using it takes on legal responsibilities.

How does the register of deeds route work for a house?

A surviving spouse or a beneficiary can end the decedent's interest in real property by filing an application with the register of deeds. Wis. Stat. 867.046(2) lists the people who can apply: the spouse, a beneficiary of a marital property agreement, a transfer on death beneficiary, or a beneficiary of certain survivorship transfers.

  • The application for real property includes the latest property tax bill and a legal description.
  • For a joint tenancy, life estate or TOD designation, it includes a copy of the deed that created the interest.
  • Recording the application ends the decedent's interest, with the same force as a court-issued confirmation.
  • If the spouse or beneficiary does not start a confirmation proceeding within 90 days after death, any interested person may apply.

A buyer or lender who acts in good faith and pays value takes title free of estate claims and has no duty to ask whether the transfer was proper.

What deadlines do Wisconsin personal representatives face?

The court sets the deadlines in a Notice of Estate Administration Deadlines when it appoints the personal representative. The guide lists the main dates and duties:

  • The Inventory is due on the date shown in that notice, with a statutory filing fee.
  • The personal representative takes the notice to creditors to a newspaper for publication and mails a copy to each known creditor.
  • An objection, offset or counterclaim to a claim must be served and filed within 60 days after the claim was mailed or served.
  • The estate can close once the claims deadline has passed and should close within 12 months of opening.
  • An extension needs a Petition for Extension of Time (PR-1833) and an order (PR-1834).
  • If no proceedings are pending six months after the Statement to Close Estate is filed, the appointment ends.

The estate also needs a Closing Certificate for Fiduciaries, which comes from filing Schedule CC with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.

Do heirs owe a transfer fee or a condition report when they sell?

Two statutes bear on an inherited home. Transfers by will, descent or survivorship are exempt from the real estate transfer fee under s. 77.25(11). Ask the register of deeds how the fee applies to the later sale to a buyer.

Under Wis. Stat. 709.01(2)(d), fiduciaries appointed by or supervised by a court are excused from the condition report if they never occupied the property. An heir who lived in the house is in a different position and should ask a Wisconsin attorney or the buyer's closing agent whether the report applies.

The guide says the Probate Registrar supplies certified copies of the Domiciliary Letters for a nominal statutory fee, so order enough copies for the title company and the buyer. Also ask the county treasurer for the current tax bill.

More questions about Wisconsin Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I need a lawyer for probate in Wisconsin?

Not for informal administration or summary settlement. The court guide says formal administration requires an attorney and that you must be represented in proceedings before a judge. It suggests speaking with one early when a claim may need to be disallowed.

How long does Wisconsin probate take?

The guide says an estate can close once the claims deadline has passed and should close within 12 months of opening. The Probate Registrar can grant more time on a petition for extension.

Where do I file a Wisconsin probate case?

File in the county where the decedent lived at death. If the decedent was not a Wisconsin resident, any county where Wisconsin property is located can receive the application. Call that county's Register in Probate to ask about appointments.

Can I sell the house before probate is finished?

Yes, once you hold court-issued letters as personal representative and sign a deed with the full legal description. The court guide describes selling real estate as one of the personal representative's tasks. Spouses and certain beneficiaries may instead use the register of deeds route in Wis. Stat. 867.046.

What is the small estate limit in Wisconsin?

The limit is $50,000 in gross value. That figure appears in Wis. Stat. 867.03(1g) for the transfer by affidavit and in the court guide for summary settlement and summary assignment.

  • A deed given in fulfillment of a land contract is exempt from the transfer fee if the fee was paid when the land contract (or evidence of it) was recorded. (Wis. Stat. 77.25(17); source)
  • The seller condition report requirement applies to transfers by sale, exchange or land contract of 1-4 unit property. (Wis. Stat. 709.01(1); source)

Wisconsin Land Contracts: Seller Rules FAQ

What is a land contract?

A contract where the buyer pays over time while the seller keeps title until a set point.

How does a land contract sale work in Wisconsin?

A Wisconsin land contract lets a buyer pay the seller over time, and a deed follows once the contract is fulfilled. The seller is the vendor and the buyer is the purchaser or vendee, and the statutes and court decisions use those labels.

The contract has to be in writing. Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(e) says a contract to convey is not valid unless it is signed by or on behalf of all parties. A handshake deal or an unsigned payment ledger will not carry a property transfer.

Even though the vendor holds the deed, the vendee has real rights. The Wisconsin Supreme Court held in Steiner v. Wisconsin American Mutual Insurance Company, 2005 WI 72, that equitable title stays with the vendee until a circuit court enters an order confirming default after the redemption period ends. The official annotations to s. 846.30 summarize that holding.

What happens if the buyer stops paying on a land contract?

The vendor has to go to court, and the court must give the buyer at least 7 working days to redeem. Wis. Stat. 846.30 covers strict foreclosure of a land contract. If the court finds the buyer owes payments and failed to make them, and the vendor is entitled to strict foreclosure, it sets a redemption period of at least 7 working days from the judgment hearing or, with no hearing, from entry of the judgment order.

No strict foreclosure judgment is final until the court enters an order after the redemption period confirming that no redemption occurred. Only then does the judgment become absolute.

The annotations add that the minimum period exists to keep a court from giving the buyer no chance to redeem. A court of appeals decision listed there also holds that the right can be waived when every person who holds it agrees to waive.

Because the buyer's rights end only through that court order, a vendor who wants out of a stalled contract should ask the clerk of circuit court in the county where the property sits how a strict foreclosure case starts and what filing fee applies.

What transfer fee applies to a Wisconsin land contract?

The grantor owes the state real estate transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction, which is $3 per $1,000. Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) adds that for a land contract the value is the total principal amount the buyer agrees to pay the seller.

As an illustration only, a land contract with total principal of $120,000 produces a fee of $360 at that rate. The register of deeds collects the fee when the instrument is submitted for recording, and the grantor and grantee both sign the transfer return.

SituationFee treatmentSource
Land contract recordedFee based on total principal the buyer agrees to payWis. Stat. 77.22(1)
Deed given when the contract is paidExempt if the proper fee was paid when the contract or evidence of it was recordedWis. Stat. 77.25(17)
Foreclosure or deed in lieu to a land contract sellerExemptWis. Stat. 77.25(14)
Transfer by will, descent or survivorshipExemptWis. Stat. 77.25(11)
Fee collectionRegister of deeds collects it at recording, with a return signed by grantor and granteeWis. Stat. 77.22(1)

The definition in s. 77.21(1) counts contracts and assignments of a vendee's interest as conveyances. If a buyer sells their position to someone else, ask the register of deeds how the fee applies to that assignment.

Which disclosures must a land contract seller give?

A seller of one-to-four unit residential property by land contract must give the buyer a condition report. Wis. Stat. 709.01(1) applies the disclosure rules to transfers by sale, exchange or land contract, unless the transfer is exempt from the transfer fee.

  • The report is due no later than 10 days after acceptance of the contract of sale or option contract.
  • A buyer who gets no report in that time may rescind in writing within 2 business days after the 10-day period ends and recover deposits.
  • A report counts as complete only when the owner answered or supplied information for every item.
  • Personal representatives, trustees, conservators and court-supervised fiduciaries who never occupied the property are excused from the report.

Condominium sellers must add the association name, assessment amounts and a contact person to the report.

What if a land contract vendor or vendee dies?

The vendor's interest can pass through the register of deeds, without a court case, when the right person applies. Under Wis. Stat. 867.046(2), the decedent's spouse, a beneficiary of a marital property agreement, a transfer on death beneficiary, or a beneficiary of certain survivorship transfers can apply to the register of deeds in the county where the property sits.

  • The application for real property includes a copy of the latest property tax bill and a legal description.
  • When recorded, the application serves as prima facie evidence of the facts it recites and ends the decedent's interest.
  • If no one starts a confirmation proceeding within 90 days after death, any interested person may apply.
  • A purchaser or lender who acts in good faith and pays value takes title free of estate claims and has no duty to inquire.

Ask the register of deeds in your county for the application form and whether the office accepts it in person or by mail.

Can a land contract buyer get Wisconsin property tax credits?

A land contract buyer can qualify for the lottery and gaming credit when the home is a primary residence. The Department of Revenue says the buyer qualifies if the land contract, or an instrument evidencing it, is notarized no later than six months after the January 1 certification date.

The same page says the credit stays with a property that is sold after January 1 and should be counted when taxes are prorated between buyer and seller. The county treasurer where the property sits can tell you whether the credit appears on the current bill.

The annotations to s. 815.20 also state that a land contract vendee has an interest sufficient to support the homestead exemption, which protects up to $75,000 against creditors.

What should a land contract seller do before selling the home?

Pull the paperwork first, then decide whether to wait for the contract to finish or sell the vendor's position. A cash buyer will want to see the signed contract, the payment history and any recorded memorandum.

  • Ask the register of deeds whether the contract or a notice of it is recorded, and whether the transfer fee return was filed.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the tax bill and any credit shown on it.
  • Read the contract for any clause that limits assignment or sale before you promise anything to a new buyer.
  • Ask the county treasurer whether any taxes are past due on the parcel.

A Wisconsin real estate attorney can tell you whether strict foreclosure or a negotiated payoff fits your facts.

More questions about Wisconsin Land Contracts and Contracts for Deed

How long does a buyer have to redeem after a land contract judgment in Wisconsin?

The court must set a redemption period of at least 7 working days. Wis. Stat. 846.30 counts it from the judgment hearing or, with no hearing, from entry of the judgment order. The judgment is not final until a later order confirms that no redemption happened.

Who pays the transfer fee on a land contract?

The grantor pays it. The rate is 30 cents per $100 of value, and for a land contract the value is the total principal the buyer agrees to pay the seller. The register of deeds collects it at recording.

Is a land contract sale exempt from the condition report?

No, unless the transfer is exempt from the transfer fee or the seller is an excused fiduciary who never lived there. Wis. Stat. 709.01(1) names land contracts among the covered transfers for one-to-four unit property.

Does the buyer own the house during a land contract?

The buyer holds equitable title. A 2005 Wisconsin Supreme Court decision says equitable title stays with the buyer until a court order confirms default after the redemption period ends.

Can heirs of a land contract vendor sell the property?

They can once their interest is confirmed. The register of deeds route under Wis. Stat. 867.046 lets qualifying beneficiaries record an application, and a good-faith purchaser from them takes free of estate claims.

What the official sources say
